rationale: A narrow pass with one decisive retrieval and one incidental one. The 2025 runners' elastography study, which the edition ranks first among unretrieved primaries and names as 'Olewnik 2025', was retrieved in full from PubMed Central: its first author is Landfald (Podgórski and Olewnik follow), it is a prospective single-centre cohort with no control arm, and it reports that after one course of thumb compression, given with no breathing instruction anywhere in its methods, most palpated gastrocnemius trigger points were undetectable by palpation and strain elastography and none of the eliminated points recurred at 24 hours. That is the ledger's first objective imaged record of a fast, persistent change at a palpated knot. It supports VASO-C011 (the change is a change of state, whatever the state), undermines VASO-C039 as written (pressure without breath instruction sufficed), and qualifies VASO-C004; the caveat that breathing was uncontrolled and unrecorded is stated in every record and is the reason the strength is moderate, not decisive. It took no Doppler and had no sham arm, so nothing in it touches the vascular attribution (VASO-C020, VASO-C073) or the perforator picture; the stiff foci it imaged lie inside the muscle belly. Second, the report saw only a snippet of Croft, Schollum & Silman 1994, but I was shown the PMC abstract with Results: two general practices, an 18-site count, medians of six in women and three in men, and depression, fatigue and sleep scores rising with count independently of pain. That gives VASO-C083, C085, C086, C087 and C088 their first primary — with the important limitation, stated in each record, that the examined subsample was selected on reported pain, so the medians are not unselected community medians and the survey cannot speak to 'nearly universal' (VASO-C084, qualified). Six new observation claims are catalogued from the two sources, one proposition each. One correction removes the retrieved study from VASO-R012's title and fixes the attribution. One new research item specifies the test the two retrievals make decisive: the compression protocol repeated with breathing recorded and randomised among free breathing, slow exhale and inhale-and-hold, with an elastography endpoint. I could not write the report's proposed sharpening of VASO-R001/VASO-R003 as a correction because the packet does not show those records' current summary text, and the schema carries no image records, so the CC BY-NC-ND figure is dispositioned blocked with its route. The edition is left unchanged: the verdict does not move, and the article's conditional paragraph on the runners' study should be rewritten only after these records are verified and admitted; the change is load-bearing enough that the next edition pass should do so, and should correct 'Olewnik' to 'Landfald and colleagues' throughout.

sources.title: Ultrasound elastography to guide compression therapy for gastrocnemius trigger points in runners
reliabilityNotes: Peer-reviewed primary (Scientific Reports 15:41950, 25 Nov 2025), full text read at PMC12647689; the publisher DOI page served a bot-challenge page.
Prospective, single-centre cohort of 30 amateur runners with gastrocnemius trigger points (from 44 screened); no control, sham or comparison arm; strain (compression) elastography, not shear-wave.

The radiologist was blinded to treatment outcomes but not to the initial palpation findings; elastography cine loops were not archived; no colour/power Doppler was performed; imaging plane at follow-up may have differed (authors' own limitations).
The methods describe compression in 30-s bouts with 10-s rests; no breathing instruction is described or recorded anywhere in the text.
Independent of the NIH (Shah/Ballyns) and Hubbard/Gevirtz lineages; the Mazovian Academy in Płock and Medical University of Łódź.
Licence stated in the text: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International; © The Author(s) 2025.

sources.title: Population study of tender point counts and pain as evidence of fibromyalgia
reliabilityNotes: Peer-reviewed primary (BMJ 309:696–699, 17 Sep 1994); only the structured abstract was retrieved at PMC2540791 (full text is a scanned PDF not shown).

Two-stage cross-sectional design in two general practices in north-west England; a stratified random sample answered a pain questionnaire, and 250 responders were selected for tender-point examination on the basis of their reported pain complaints, of whom 177 participated. The examined subsample is therefore pain-selected, not an unselected community sample.
Outcome is the 18-site tender-point count (0–18) of the 1990 ACR fibromyalgia criteria; tissue damage is not assessed or mentioned in the abstract.
Arthritis and Rheumatism Council Epidemiology Research Unit, University of Manchester; independent of the trigger-point lineages in the ledger.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: most palpated gastrocnemius trigger points undetectable by palpation and elastography after one compression course, none recurring at 24 hours
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that in 30 runners with 103 gastrocnemius trigger points identified by palpation, thumb compression in 30-s bouts with 10-s rests, up to three rounds, made most points disappear from both palpation and strain elastography by the end of the first course: "After the first compression course, 75/103 MTrPs were no longer detectable." A further 21 were visible only on elastography with reduced stiffness and area, and 7 remained. At follow-up the next day, "none of the 75 eliminated or 21 elastography-only MTrPs recurred".
evidence.editorInference: This is the ledger's first objective, imaged record of a palpated stiff focus disappearing within minutes and staying gone for a day. A change on that timescale is a change of maintained state, not of remodelled structure — the inference the claim states — whatever the state turns out to be; all three accounts in the case predict this result and none is distinguished by it. Strength is moderate rather than strong because there is no control or sham arm, the elastography is strain (semi-quantitative) rather than shear-wave, and the reassessment was after each course rather than time-resolved.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Abstract; Results paragraph beginning 'Seventy-five out of 103 recognized MTrPs'; Results 'During the examination on the following day'
limitations: No control, sham or no-treatment arm; expectation and generalised relaxation are not excluded.
Strain elastography with operator-applied compression; stiffness ratios are relative, not absolute moduli.
Radiologist blinded to treatment outcomes but not to initial palpation findings; imaging plane at follow-up may have differed slightly (authors' limitations).
Reassessment after each compression course, not time-resolved; nothing here bears on the seconds-scale time-lock or on what tissue changed.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: pressure with no breathing instruction sufficed to make most trigger points undetectable
evidence.sourceStatement: The source's release protocol is manual pressure only: "a strong compression (resulting in pain) transferred by tips of both thumbs was applied in 30-s intervals", and between compressions "10 s of rest was applied to allow for blood re-perfusion". No breathing instruction, recording or manipulation appears anywhere in the methods or results. Under that protocol, "After the first compression course, 75/103 MTrPs were no longer detectable."
evidence.editorInference: The claim's own truth condition makes it false if pressure alone suffices; here pressure without any breath manipulation sufficed for about three-quarters of points immediately and for all but two at 24 hours. This is direct contrary evidence. It does not close the claim, because breathing was neither instructed nor recorded: subjects under painful sustained pressure may have exhaled slowly on their own, so 'no breath instruction' is not 'breath held constant'. That reply is testable by the inhale-and-hold block, which is why the record is moderate and not decisive.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Materials and methods, 'MTrP release'; Abstract
limitations: Breathing uncontrolled and unrecorded, so a spontaneous slow exhale under pressure cannot be excluded.
The endpoint is palpation and elastography, not the felt release the two-key protocol describes.
Different muscle (gastrocnemius) and population (symptomatic amateur runners) from the practitioner reports behind the claim.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: objective disappearance of trigger points under pressure alone, without the breath component
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports objective disappearance of palpated trigger points after compression alone — "After the first compression course, 75/103 MTrPs were no longer detectable." — under a protocol in which compression was "applied in 30-s intervals" with 10-s rests and no breathing instruction is described. Pain scores during compression fell over the course.
evidence.editorInference: The claim states that pressure combined with slow exhalation can produce a felt release within seconds. This record does not deny that; it shows that the objective correlate (loss of the stiff, palpable focus) can be produced by pressure without any breath instruction, so the exhale is at most a facilitator or a felt correlate rather than a demonstrated necessary component. The record says nothing about the felt release itself or about seconds.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Abstract; Materials and methods, 'MTrP release'
limitations: No felt-release event was recorded; the endpoint is palpation, elastography and a pain score after each course.
Breathing uncontrolled and unrecorded.
Timescale is minutes per course, not seconds.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: active trigger points larger, stiffer and more painful than latent ones; latent ones cleared more often after one round
evidence.sourceStatement: The source classified 67 points as active and 36 as latent and reports that active points had higher pain scores, larger cross-sectional area and "greater stiffness ratios (mean 8.5 vs. 6.1", with all three differences significant; in the discussion, "active points were larger, stiffer, and more painful". After the first round, "60% of ATrPs and 86% of LTrPs were no longer detectable sonographically" (p = 0.021). Before compression, points were 4.7 to 13.8 times stiffer than surrounding tissue, and stiffness correlated with pain (Spearman rho = 0.61).
evidence.editorInference: A second laboratory, a second muscle (gastrocnemius) and a second elastography method (strain rather than vibration) reproduce the graded finding that palpated points are measurably stiffer than surrounding tissue and that the more symptomatic class is stiffer still. The record has no palpably normal control sites and no biochemistry or Doppler, so it supports the stiffness component of the claim only.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Results, 'Comparison between active and latent MTrPs' and Table 2; Discussion
limitations: No palpably normal or pain-free control sites; the comparison is active versus latent within symptomatic runners.
Subgroup analyses described by the authors as exploratory and underpowered.
Strain elastography stiffness ratios are relative, operator-dependent measures.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: active/latent differences in a second muscle as context for the graded-stiffness and fresh/old claims
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that in the gastrocnemius "active points were larger, stiffer, and more painful" than latent points, and that latent points "were more often resolved after the first treatment"; active points required more sessions to deactivate (1.4 versus 1.1). The authors suggest that latent points may represent earlier or less fibrotic lesions, and call for confirmation in controlled studies.
evidence.editorInference: For the trapezius vibration-elastography gradient this is a parallel from another muscle and method, not a replication. For the fresh/old claims it is the nearest instrumented cousin — the more symptomatic point is harder to switch off — but active/latent is a clinical classification, not the age of the knot, so the record carries no weight for or against those claims.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Results, Table 2; Discussion paragraph beginning 'Additionally, our subgroup analysis'
limitations: Different muscle, method and site classes from the trapezius sonoelastography study.
Active/latent is not the fresh/old axis; the authors' 'earlier or less fibrotic' reading is their conjecture.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: about a quarter of palpated hard spots had no imaging correlate
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that palpation identified a mean of 4.7 points per runner while ultrasound confirmed a mean of 3.4: "Elastography confirmed the presence of only some of these". In the discussion, "it confirmed 71.5% of palpated hard spots as MTrPs", the remainder corresponding to tendinous cores or musculotendinous junctions. Gastrocnemius trigger points were diagnosed in 30 of 44 symptomatic runners screened (68%).
evidence.editorInference: Tender points were common in this cohort, but it is a symptomatic, self-selected group, so the 68% is not a population figure and should not be read as one. That roughly a quarter of palpated spots lacked an imaging correlate narrows what 'discrete, palpable' can mean under the fingertip; it is compatible both with palpation false positives and with imaging insensitivity, and the authors say ultrasound is not an established gold standard.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Results paragraph beginning 'In the 30 participants with MTrPs'; Discussion; Abstract
limitations: Symptomatic, self-selected running cohort; no population sampling.
Imaging is not a validated reference standard for trigger points (authors' own limitation), so the gap could be imaging insensitivity.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: no gold standard for detecting trigger points; palpation variability the authors' stated reason for adding imaging
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that "there is no gold standard technique for detecting them" and that manual palpation "has significant inter-observer variability that cannot be meaningfully improved after training", citing earlier reliability work; this is the authors' rationale for combining B-mode ultrasound and strain elastography with palpation. In their own data, imaging confirmed 71.5% of palpated hard spots.
evidence.editorInference: A proponent-side clinical group states the reliability problem in its own words and reports a concrete palpation–imaging discrepancy. Weak because the reliability statement is a citation of others rather than a new measurement, and because the authors did not test their own inter- or intra-observer reliability.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Discussion paragraph beginning 'Although the removal of MTrPs'; Limitations
limitations: The inter-observer-variability statement is secondary (cites earlier work).
No formal reliability testing of the sonographic assessment was performed (authors' limitation).

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: no Doppler was performed, so the order of perfusion and stiffness change was not observed
evidence.sourceStatement: The source's limitations state that "Systematic color/power Doppler assessment was not performed" and that elastography cine loops were not archived; reassessment was after each compression course, not time-resolved during it.
evidence.editorInference: The one imaged fast change of a trigger point the ledger now holds carries no flow channel and no time resolution, so it bears on the blood-first ordering only by showing the design that would need to be extended — the same region imaged with Doppler and archived cine during the compression and release. Zero weight for or against the claim.
limitations: Absence of a measurement is not evidence about the ordering; this record is background only.

evidence.title: Landfald 2025: the authors' reperfusion rationale for compression is stated, not measured
evidence.sourceStatement: The source describes the likely mechanism of ischemic compression as "transient local ischemia during compression followed by hyperemic reperfusion after release", with increased blood flow supporting aerobic metabolism, and built its protocol's 10-s rests "to allow for blood re-perfusion" — while performing no Doppler or perfusion measurement.
evidence.editorInference: The vascular vocabulary is already in the clinicians' account of why compression works, but it is asserted, not measured, and it is a reperfusion-of-compressed-muscle story rather than a smooth-muscle latch. It neither supports nor undermines the latched-arteriole attribution.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC12647689, Discussion paragraph beginning 'As the diagnostic criteria for MTrPs are not standardized'; Materials and methods, 'MTrP release'
limitations: Mechanism statement is secondary (cites earlier work) and unmeasured in this study.

evidence.title: Croft 1994: the 18-site tender-point count applied in a community general-practice sample
evidence.sourceStatement: The source is a two-stage cross-sectional study set in "Two general practices in north west England", drawing a stratified random sample of adults from age–sex registers, in which 177 selected responders underwent tender-point examination with the outcome "Tender point count (0 to 18) grouped into four categories", the highest (11 or more) corresponding to the ACR fibromyalgia criteria.
evidence.editorInference: This is the primary the founding essay gestured at: the fibromyalgia-era 18-site exam administered outside the clinic. Note that the examined subsample was chosen on reported pain complaints, so it is a community-based but pain-selected sample.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC2540791, Abstract (Design, Setting, Subjects, Main outcome measures)
limitations: Abstract only retrieved; full text not shown.
Examined subsample (177 of 250 selected) was chosen on the basis of reported pain complaints.

evidence.title: Croft 1994: median tender-point count six in women and three in men
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that women had a "higher median tender point count (six) than did men (three)" among the 177 adults examined, and that counts were higher in those with pain than without, and in widespread than regional pain.
evidence.editorInference: These are the medians the founding essay quoted. They are from a sample selected for examination on reported pain complaints, so they are not unselected community medians and probably overstate the general population; the essay's phrase 'community samples' is accurate as to setting but not as to selection.
limitations: Examined subsample pain-selected; medians are not from an unselected population.
Abstract only; sex-specific denominators and distributions not shown.

evidence.title: Croft 1994: depression, fatigue and sleep scores rise with tender-point count, independently of pain
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that mean "symptom scores for depression, fatigue, and sleep problems increased" as the tender-point count rose (P for trend < 0.001), that "These trends were independent of pain complaints", and concludes that "Tender points are a measure of general distress", separately associated with fatigue and depression; sleep problems are associated with tender points, with prospective studies needed to settle whether they cause tenderness.
evidence.editorInference: Direct primary support for the correlate structure the essay described: counts track distress and poor sleep. Cross-sectional, so direction of causation is open, as the authors say. The abstract does not measure or mention tissue damage, so it says nothing about the separate claim that counts do not track damage.
limitations: Cross-sectional; no causal direction.
Pain-selected examined subsample.
Abstract only; instruments and effect sizes not shown.

evidence.title: Croft 1994: the examined subsample was selected on reported pain, so the survey cannot speak to universality
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that of the questionnaire responders, 250 were selected for tender-point examination "on the basis of their reported pain complaints" and 177 participated; the abstract reports medians and trends but no proportion of subjects with zero tender points.
evidence.editorInference: This survey — the locatable primary behind the essay's proto-census — cannot by its design establish that tender points are nearly universal in the unselected population, and its abstract gives no zero-count proportion. If the 'nearly universal' figure exists it must come from another survey (the report names Wolfe 1995 as the likelier primary). The claim is narrowed in its evidential base, not denied.
limitations: Abstract only; the full text may report the count distribution including zeros.

evidence.title: Croft 1994: high tender-point counts in people reporting no pain
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that two people "with counts of 11 or more were in the group reporting no pain", and that most subjects with chronic widespread pain had fewer than 11 tender points (27 of 45).
evidence.editorInference: Examiner-elicited tender points occur in people with no pain complaint at all, which is the population the case's opening observation describes. Weak because it is two individuals, the sample was pain-selected, and the 18-site protocol tests fixed anatomical sites rather than counting palpable knots.
limitations: Two individuals; pain-selected subsample.
Fixed-site tenderness testing is not a census of palpable knots.

research.title: Repeat the runners' compression protocol with breathing recorded and randomised: free breathing, slow exhale, inhale-and-hold
research.summary: Take the now-verified single-session ischemic-compression protocol (30-s thumb compressions with 10-s rests, up to three rounds, palpation plus B-mode and strain or shear-wave elastography before, after each round and at 24 h) and add the one factor it left uncontrolled: breath. Record respiration continuously (inductance belt and end-tidal CO2) and randomise each trigger point within a participant to one of three conditions during compression — free breathing, instructed slow exhalation, or pressure applied only during an inhale-and-hold — with sham compression at a matched non-tender site as a fourth arm and a no-treatment point followed at the same time points. Measure, per point, whether the stiff focus is undetectable after the session and at 24 h, its stiffness ratio and cross-sectional area, and the pain score. Decision rule: if the elimination rate under inhale-and-hold is no lower than under free breathing, the breath is not a necessary key and the two-key claim fails; if inhale-and-hold blocks elimination while slow exhalation matches or exceeds free breathing, the breath-gating the perforator account predicts is real; if all three active arms exceed sham and no-treatment equally, pressure alone suffices and the felt release is a correlate. Archive cine loops and, where available, add power Doppler over the same region so the order of perfusion and stiffness change can be read.
research.informationGain: The ledger's only objective record of a fast release was obtained with breathing uninstructed and unrecorded, so it undermines the two-key claim without closing it. One session per participant with the breath factor randomised separates the three readings — breath necessary, breath gating, breath irrelevant — and, with the sham and no-treatment arms, separates the compression effect from expectation and regression. A positive inhale-hold block would be the first evidence for breath-gated release in any tissue; a null would return the exhale to the status of a felt correlate and move the case's anchor observation onto pressure alone.
